source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 6 (i)-(ii): perpendicular pairs by dot product, parallel pairs by multiples / cross product (book p.283). Answer key PDF 312.

blocks.prompt: 6 (i) Which vectors, if any, are perpendicular or parallel: \(\underline{u} = 5\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\); \(\underline{v} = \underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\); \(\underline{w} = -15\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
A test of perpendicular and parallel pairs.
We must check the three pairs \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}\); \(\underline{u}, \underline{w}\); \(\underline{v}, \underline{w}\).
Plan: dot product 0 means perpendicular; cross product \(\underline{0}\) (one vector a multiple of the other) means parallel.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 5\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = \underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = -15\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\).
To find: perpendicular pairs and parallel pairs.
Method: Non-zero vectors are perpendicular iff their dot product is 0 (14.2.6), and parallel iff their cross product is \(\underline{0}\) (14.3.2), that is, one is a scalar multiple of the other.

Dot products of the three pairs
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (5)(0) + (-1)(1) + (1)(-5)\]
\[= 0 - 1 - 5 = -6\]
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{w} = (5)(-15) + (-1)(3) + (1)(-3)\]
\[= -75 - 3 - 3 = -81\]
\[\underline{v} \cdot \underline{w} = (0)(-15) + (1)(3) + (-5)(-3)\]
\[= 0 + 3 + 15 = 18\]
Why: None of them is 0, so no pair is perpendicular. (Note \(\underline{v} = 0\underline{i} + \underline{j} - 5\underline{k}\).)

Look for a multiple
\[\underline{w} = -15\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\]
\[= -3(5\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}) = -3\underline{u}\]
Why: Taking out the common factor \(-3\) shows \(\underline{w}\) is \(-3\) times \(\underline{u}\): same line, opposite direction.

Write the determinant
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{w} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 5 & -1 & 1 \\ -15 & 3 & -3 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1 holds the unit vectors, row 2 the components of the first vector \(\underline{u}\), row 3 those of the second \(\underline{w}\). The order of the rows follows the order of the product.

Work out the three minors
\[\underline{i}\text{ minor} = (-1)(-3) - (1)(3) = 0\]
\[\underline{j}\text{ minor} = (5)(-3) - (1)(-15) = 0\]
\[\underline{k}\text{ minor} = (5)(3) - (-1)(-15) = 0\]
Why: For each unit vector cover its row and column; the minor is (top-left)(bottom-right) minus (top-right)(bottom-left).

Attach the signs \(+, -, +\)
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{w} = \underline{i}(0) - \underline{j}(0) + \underline{k}(0)\]
\[= \underline{0}\]
Why: Expanding a determinant along row 1 uses the sign pattern \(+, -, +\); the middle (\(\underline{j}\)) term is subtracted.

The other pairs are not parallel
\[\underline{u}, \underline{v}:\ \text{first components } 5, 0\]
\[\underline{v}, \underline{w}:\ \text{first components } 0, -15\]
Why: \(\underline{v}\) has first component 0 but \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{w}\) do not, so \(\underline{v}\) cannot be a multiple of either (a multiple of 0 is 0, and \(\underline{v} \ne \underline{0}\)).

blocks.prompt: 6 (ii) Which vectors, if any, are perpendicular or parallel: \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\); \(\underline{v} = -\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \underline{k}\); \(\underline{w} = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{i} - \pi\underline{j} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Same type as part (i).
We check the three pairs for dot product 0 (perpendicular) and for being multiples (parallel).
Plan: three dot products, then look for a common factor.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = -\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{i} - \pi\underline{j} + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{k}\).
To find: perpendicular pairs and parallel pairs.
Method: dot product 0 means perpendicular; a scalar multiple (cross product \(\underline{0}\)) means parallel.

Dot products of the three pairs
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (1)(-1) + (2)(1) + (-1)(1)\]
\[= -1 + 2 - 1 = 0\]
\[\underline{v} \cdot \underline{w} = (-1)\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + (1)(-\pi) + (1)\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\]
\[= \tfrac{\pi}{2} - \pi + \tfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\]
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{w} = (1)\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + (2)(-\pi) + (-1)\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\]
\[= -\tfrac{\pi}{2} - 2\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{2} = -3\pi\]
Why: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\) and \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{w} = 0\): these pairs are perpendicular. \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{w} \ne 0\).

Look for a multiple
\[\underline{w} = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{i} - \pi\underline{j} + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\underline{k}\]
\[= -\tfrac{\pi}{2}(\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}) = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\underline{u}\]
Why: The common factor \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) leaves exactly \(\underline{u}\), so \(\underline{w}\) is parallel to \(\underline{u}\).

Confirm with the cross product
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{w} = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}(\underline{u} \times \underline{u})\]
\[= -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\underline{0} = \underline{0}\]
Why: A scalar comes out of a cross product, and \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \underline{0}\).

Check the logic
Why: \(\underline{v} \perp \underline{u}\) and \(\underline{w}\) lies along \(\underline{u}\), so \(\underline{v} \perp \underline{w}\) must also hold; the zero dot product above agrees. \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are not multiples (\(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\) for non-zero vectors rules that out).
